feedback: If a learner says there's no gravity in space: gravity reaches out across space — it is exactly what holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun.
If a learner ties gravity to air: gravity acts in the airless vacuum of space too — the Moon has gravity and no air at all.
Prompt: 'What keeps the Moon circling instead of drifting off in a straight line?' (Earth's gravity continually bending its path.)
activities.intendedInsight: Gravity is a long-reach attraction acting across empty space — no air or contact needed. The same pull that makes a ball fall is what bends the Moon's straight-line motion into an orbit around Earth, and the planets' paths around the Sun.
learnerActions: Study (or manipulate) a diagram of the Moon circling Earth with a gravity arrow pointing from the Moon toward Earth.

Predict: 'If the pull between Earth and Moon suddenly switched off, what path would the Moon take?' Then check in the simple Earth–Moon model (ignoring the Sun's pull) — with the pull off, the Moon moves off in a straight (tangent) line; with the pull on, that same pull curves its path into an orbit.
Repeat the idea with a Sun-at-centre diagram: each planet has a gravity arrow pointing at the Sun.
State in your own words how the force that drops a ball on Earth is the SAME force that keeps the Moon and planets in orbit.
Explain whether gravity needs air to work, using the airless Moon as evidence.
activities.title: Same pull drops a ball and bends the Moon's path

feedback: If a learner says gravity has switched off in space: the same pull holds the Moon in orbit; if gravity were gone, the ship and astronaut would fly off in a straight line, not circle Earth.
Reinforce that the astronaut and spacecraft fall together, so the astronaut appears to float relative to the craft.
Label the image honestly as 'still lots of gravity — falling around Earth', not 'zero gravity'.
activities.intendedInsight: Astronauts float because they are in continual free-fall (orbit) around Earth, where Earth's gravity is still strong — not because gravity has vanished. 'Weightlessness' is free-fall, not absence of gravity.
learnerActions: Look at an image of an astronaut floating and discuss WHY they float.
Decide which explanation fits the evidence: (a) gravity has switched off, or (b) the astronaut and their ship are both falling around Earth together, with Earth's gravity still strongly acting.
Connect this to the orbit idea: being in orbit IS continual free-fall around Earth.
Answer: 'Is there gravity where astronauts are? How do you know?'
activities.title: Busting the 'zero gravity' myth

feedback: Full understanding: explains gravity pulls toward Earth's centre so 'down' is centre-relative (opposite sides both feel normal), AND that the same pull keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits.

Partial: says gravity pulls 'down' and nobody falls off, but cannot clearly state 'down' means toward the centre, or doesn't connect gravity to orbits — revisit the arrow-drawing and orbit activities.
Gap: thinks the far side is upside-down and could fall off, or that there's no gravity in space — return to placing figures around the globe and drawing each 'down' arrow to the centre.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain WHY no one falls off — because 'down' is centre-relative, not absolute — is the crux. A learner who still holds an absolute 'down' thinks the far side hangs upside-down; a learner who understands the concept says everyone's feet point 'down' toward the centre and no one falls.
learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'A child in Australia is on nearly the opposite side of the round Earth from a child in Britain. Are the people in Australia hanging upside down, in danger of falling off into space? What does "down" actually mean for them? Tell me WHY.'
Decide: is there one single 'down' for the whole universe, or does 'down' depend on where you're standing?
Match each cause to its effect: Earth's pull → a ball falls toward the centre; Earth's pull → the Moon orbits; the Sun's pull → planets orbit.
Judge true or false and justify: 'There is no gravity in space.'
activities.title: Check and reason: which way is 'down'?
